newsitem.title: USA: Bosnia envoy Holbrooke named to tackle Cyprus feud.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia envoy Holbrooke named to tackle Cyprus feud.

text.p: President Bill Clinton appointed Richard Holbrooke, who mediated the Bosnian peace deal, as his special emissary for Cyprus on Wednesday amid fresh efforts to settle the dispute on the divided island.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the appointment represented "a rebirth and a renewal" of the U.S. mediation effort between the Greek and Turkish communities, divided since 1974.
"This appointment of one of our most capable negotiators demonstrates our commitment to help promote a final political settlement on Cyprus," Burns told reporters.

Holbrooke, out of government service for more than a year, will replace Richard Beattie, named by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright last month as her adviser on incorporating three foreign affairs agencies into the State Department.
Burns said the United States had no illusions about the toughness and complexity of the challenge. "That is why we are bringing in our toughest negotiator," he said.

Holbrooke himself played down prospects of rapid success. "I don't want to leave you with the idea that we have the magic bullet," he told Reuters in a telephone interview from Copenhagen, where he is on a visit.
"Given the present political situation in Turkey, it's not clear to me what can be accomplished. But the Turks have said they want U.S. involvement, so we'll give it our best shot."
Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan last weekend announced a plan to go to early elections under a caretaker government, but did not set a date for polling.

President Glafkos Clerides of Cyprus and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash are due to meet on July 9 in New York for U.N.-sponsored talks. Burns said Washington strongly urged all parties to work for a comprehensive, permanent settlement on the island.
Holbrooke said he did not plan to visit the region until after the New York talks, which he would not attend.
"The president and the secretary of state are very committed to this and that's why I agreed to do it," he said. He said he had not discussed how long his mission would last.

Holbrooke, outspoken, blunt and dogged, made his name by pressuring warring Balkan forces to reach peace agreements to end the 43-month Bosnia war at Dayton, Ohio, in 1995. In February of last year he resigned as assistant secretary of state to work for Credit Suisse First Boston bank in New York.
Burns said he would not take the Cyprus post on a full-time basis. He would work on it about one week a month, retaining his main job with the bank, and appoint a negotiating team to work full-time.
Burns dismissed suggestions that there could be a conflict of interest between Holbrooke's diplomatic assignment and his banking responsibilities.
"For the period of time when he is the president's special emissary for Cyprus, he will not be conducting any business interests in this part of the world," he said.

The New York talks between Clerides and Denktash, whose Turkish Cypriot breakaway state in northern Cyprus is recognised only by Ankara, will be their first face-to-face encounter for nearly three years.

Some 30,000 Turkish troops have been stationed in northern Cyprus since Turkey invaded the island in 1974 in response to a short-lived coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Since taking office in January, Albright has said several times that she will devote high priority to Cyprus, a problem that has defeated peace-makers for more than two decades.

U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson said in New York that with the appointment of Holbrooke, who was nominated for but failed to win the Nobel Peace Prize last year, "I think we are going to see some movement on Cyprus".

Britain, which appointed its own Cyprus envoy, former U.N. ambassador Sir David Hannay, a year ago, also welcomed the appointment, saying a "concerted international effort" was needed to resolve the dispute.
